title: Summer's heat
hookLine: the hot months burn the one who is apart (Tukhari Barah Maha)

cards: Noon, and the road shimmers. A dog lies flat in the one strip of shade by the wall. Nobody walks if they don't have to.
Guru Nanak's year walks straight into that heat. Two months, Jeth and Asarh, and in both the earth is burning. Yet read closely, and the poem calls the months good.

teach.h: JETH: THE LANDS BURN LIKE A FURNACE.
teach.b: Jeth first, in plain English, not word for word. The month of Jeth is good. How could the Beloved be forgotten?
The lands are hot as a furnace, and the bride offers her prayer. Then Asarh, heavier still. The sun blazes in the sky.
The earth suffers and dries out, roasted by fire. The sun doesn't give up its work; its chariot keeps circling. The bride looks for shade.
Out in the wild, a cricket calls. Three things to notice.

teach.h: STILL, THE MONTH IS CALLED GOOD.
teach.b: First, the months are still called good. Nanak isn't complaining about summer; heat is the month doing what it does, like the sun at its work. Second, the heat pictures something inside.
The earth is parched, and so is the bride.

teach.h: THE INNER HEAT OF BEING APART.
teach.b: Being apart from the one you love has its own dryness, a thirst a glass of water can't touch. Third, look at what she does. In Jeth she prays.

In Asarh she looks for shade. She doesn't pretend she's fine, and she doesn't give up; she moves toward the one cool place there is. In Sikh reading, that shade is the Beloved's nearness, the remembrance of God's Name.
And the stanza keeps one small detail for the end: a cricket calling in the heat. The bride hears it. She's calling too.
That's today's line: the heat of apart.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in kirtan and read it in the Guru Granth Sahib, hearing the bride's longing in the hot months as the soul's thirst for God's nearness.

o: the dry ache of being apart, pictured as summer heat
a summer festival when farmers rest from the fields
the hottest month, kept as a season of fasting

games.q: what's in the hot months — tap the pairs.
p: the lands hot as a furnace
the sun blazes, the earth dries

s: Guru Nanak calls the hot months bad
he calls Jeth and Asarh good. the burning that matters is being apart.
in Asarh, the bride looks for shade
she doesn't pretend she's fine; she moves toward the one cool place.
the poem says water is enough to cure the bride's thirst
her dryness is being apart from the Beloved, a thirst water can't reach.

games.q: it's Asarh. the sun blazes and the earth is roasting. you're the bride. what does the poem show you doing?
games.why: the bride looks for shade while a cricket calls in the wild; in Sikh reading, that shade is nearness to God.

practice: Pour a glass of water, or run a little cool water over your wrists, and feel the coolness as your breath slows.
As it fades, notice any dry or heated place in you today, a worry, a distance from someone, a thirst you can name, and let the cool and the thirst sit side by side without fixing anything.
If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath, like stepping into shade.

wordCard.voice: Summer's heat. In Guru Nanak's Jeth and Asarh, the earth burns, the months are still called good, and the bride, parched by being apart, looks for shade. Today's word.

orig.note: chhaia: shade, what the bride looks for in the heat of Asarh.

carryVoice: Your line: the heat of apart. Even in the burning months, there is shade. See you tomorrow.
